item.title: How Alternative Funds Are Owned and How Managers Get Paid
item.summary: Most private funds are set up as partnerships in which investors supply the money and a manager runs it for a management fee plus a share of profits. Knowing the fee mechanics (hurdles, catch-up, high-water marks, clawbacks) tells you what the investor really keeps and what incentives the manager faces.

sections.heading: Who owns what: the partnership structure
sections.body_markdown:
Hedge funds, private equity, and private credit funds are commonly organized as **limited partnerships**. Think of a restaurant where one person runs the kitchen and takes the day-to-day decisions, while outside backers put up the cash.

- The **general partner (GP)** is the manager. It makes the investment decisions and has **unlimited liability**.
- The **limited partners (LPs)** are the investors (pension funds, endowments, wealthy individuals). They supply capital but do not manage, and their **liability is limited**: the most they can lose is what they invested.

In closed-end funds, LPs make **capital commitments** (a promise to provide money) that the GP draws down later through **capital calls**. A newer format, the **evergreen (semi-liquid) fund**, accepts subscriptions and allows redemptions on an ongoing basis. Its fees tend to be tied to NAV rather than commitments.

sections.heading: The two layers of pay: management fee and incentive fee
sections.body_markdown:
Managers are usually paid in two layers:

1. **Management fee**: a percentage of assets (hedge funds often 1%–2% a year). It is charged whether or not the fund makes money, like a retainer. In closed-end private funds it is often based on *committed* capital during the investment period and later on *invested* capital. Evergreen funds usually charge it on invested capital or NAV.
2. **Incentive fee** (performance fee): a share of profits, often 10%–20%. In private equity and private credit it is called **carried interest** or **carry**.

The traditional headline is **"2 and 20"**: a 2% management fee and a 20% incentive fee. Large investors often negotiate lower fees, such as 1.5 and 15, in return for bigger cheques or longer lockups.

sections.heading: Protecting the investor: hurdle, catch-up, high-water mark, clawback
sections.body_markdown:
Several contract terms stop the GP from being paid too easily:

- **Hurdle rate (preferred return)**: a minimum return the investor must earn before the GP gets incentive fees. In private equity it is commonly around 8%. The hurdle is tested on the investor's return *after* management fees.
- **Hard vs. soft hurdle** (standard curriculum idea): with a *hard* hurdle the incentive fee applies only to profit *above* the hurdle. With a *soft* hurdle, once the hurdle is beaten the fee applies to *all* profit, which is effectively a full catch-up.
- **Catch-up**: after the hurdle is cleared, the GP receives all or most of the next profits until it has received its full carry share of the total profit. After that, profits are split, for example 80/20. Catch-ups can range from 0% to 100%.
- **High-water mark**: the highest NAV on which an incentive fee was previously paid. After a loss, the fund must climb back above it before new incentive fees are earned. Without it, a manager could be paid twice for the same gains.
- **Clawback**: if carry is paid deal by deal and later investments lose money, the GP has to refund the excess to the LPs so that total carry matches whole-fund performance.

A related point: hedge funds can charge incentive fees on realized *and* unrealized gains. Private equity carry is normally paid only on gains realized when deals are exited.

sections.heading: Incentives: why structure shapes behaviour
sections.body_markdown:
An incentive fee shares in profits but not in losses, so it behaves like a **call option** the manager holds on the fund's performance. Options gain value with volatility, so the fee can tempt a manager to take extra risk.

- A manager **far below the high-water mark** has little to lose and may take more risk to get back into fee territory.
- A manager **far above it** may reduce risk to lock in gains until the next fee date.

GP **co-investment** ("skin in the game"), advisory committees, carry deferral and clawbacks all aim to align the GP's interests with those of the LPs.

worked_example.problem: A hedge fund starts the year with $100 million. Before any fees its assets grow to $115 million. The fund charges a 2% management fee on beginning assets and a 20% incentive fee, calculated on profit after the management fee. The hurdle rate is 8% of beginning assets, tested on return after the management fee. Compute the investor's ending value under (a) a hard hurdle and (b) a soft hurdle (full catch-up). Ignore taxes and assume the fund is at its high-water mark at the start.
steps: Profit after management fee = $115 million − $100 million − $2 million = $13 million, a 13% return on beginning assets.
Hurdle test: 13% exceeds the 8% hurdle ($8 million), so an incentive fee is payable.
(a) Hard hurdle: the fee applies only above the hurdle. 20% × ($13 million − $8 million) = 20% × $5 million = $1.0 million.
(b) Soft hurdle: the fee applies to all profit once the hurdle is beaten. 20% × $13 million = $2.6 million.
Investor's ending value = $115 million − $2 million − incentive fee. Hard: $115 − 2 − 1.0 = $112.0 million. Soft: $115 − 2 − 2.6 = $110.4 million.
No calculator keystrokes are needed; this is simple percentage arithmetic.
worked_example.answer: Hard hurdle: incentive fee $1.0 million, investor ends with $112.0 million. Soft hurdle: incentive fee $2.6 million, investor ends with $110.4 million.

formulas.name: Management fee
formulas.where: $f_m$ is the management fee rate; the fee base is assets, committed capital, invested capital or NAV, depending on the fund terms.

formulas.name: Incentive fee with a hard hurdle
formulas.where: $f_i$ is the incentive fee rate; Profit is profit after management fee; $H$ is the hurdle rate; Base is the capital on which the hurdle is measured.

formulas.name: Incentive fee with a soft hurdle (full catch-up)
formulas.where: Same symbols as above; once the hurdle is exceeded the fee applies to all profit.

exam_traps: Confusing a hurdle rate with a high-water mark: the hurdle is a minimum return to be beaten, while the high-water mark is a prior peak value that must be recovered.
Applying the incentive fee to all profit when the question specifies a hard hurdle (the fee applies only to the excess over the hurdle).
Forgetting that the management fee is paid regardless of performance and is deducted before testing the hurdle and computing the incentive fee.
Mixing up a clawback (GP refunds excess carry to LPs) with a gate or lockup (limits investor redemptions).
Treating LPs as having unlimited liability, or the GP as shielded from liability; in a limited partnership the GP bears unlimited liability and LPs can lose only their investment.

item.stem: In a typical limited partnership used for a private investment fund, which statement about liability is most accurate?

options.text: LPs carry unlimited liability and the GP's loss is capped at its fees
options.explanation: Reverses the roles. The GP carries unlimited liability, and LP losses are limited.

options.text: The GP has unlimited liability, while LPs can lose only what they invested
options.explanation: Correct. The GP manages the fund and bears unlimited liability. LPs provide capital and their losses are capped at their investment.

options.text: Both the GP and LPs are liable for fund debts without any cap
options.explanation: Ignores the limited-liability feature that defines LPs.

item.stem: Which description best fits a hurdle rate (preferred return) in a fund's fee terms?

options.text: The return investors must earn before the GP can collect an incentive fee
options.explanation: Correct. The hurdle is a minimum investor return, tested after management fees, that must be exceeded before incentive fees are earned.

options.text: The highest NAV previously reached, which must be regained before a fee
options.explanation: Describes a high-water mark, not a hurdle rate.

options.text: The cap on total management fees the GP may charge in any year
options.explanation: A hurdle is not a fee cap. It is a performance threshold for the incentive fee.

item.stem: A private equity fund pays carried interest to the GP immediately after each deal is exited. Later, the remaining investments are written off. Which provision addresses the resulting overpayment?

options.text: A gate that postpones LP redemption requests after the lockup ends
options.explanation: Confuses a gate, which limits investor redemptions, with a provision that returns fees.

options.text: A hurdle rate that sets the minimum return before management fees
options.explanation: A hurdle applies to incentive fees, not management fees, and it does not refund carry already paid.

options.text: A clawback that returns excess carry already paid to the LPs
options.explanation: Correct. A clawback makes the GP refund earlier carry so that total carry reflects whole-fund performance.

item.stem: A hedge fund's NAV falls after a year in which an incentive fee was paid. What is the main purpose of a high-water mark?

options.text: To require a minimum annual return before any incentive fee is charged
options.explanation: Confuses the high-water mark with a hurdle rate.

options.text: To prevent new incentive fees until NAV recovers above its previous peak
options.explanation: Correct. The fund must regain the earlier peak, so investors do not pay twice for recovering the same losses.

options.text: To limit the incentive fee to a fixed percentage of committed capital
options.explanation: A high-water mark does not cap the fee. It conditions when the fee can be earned.

item.stem: A fund starts with $200 million. Its return after management fees is 12% for the year. The incentive fee is 20%, and a hard hurdle of 8% applies to beginning assets. The fund is at its high-water mark. What is the incentive fee?

options.text: $4.8 million, from applying 20% to the entire 12% profit
options.explanation: Treats the hurdle as soft with a full catch-up. With a hard hurdle the fee applies only to the excess.

options.text: $3.2 million, from applying 20% to the 8% hurdle amount only
options.explanation: Charges the fee on the hurdle portion instead of the profit above it.

options.text: $1.6 million, from 20% of the 4% excess return over the hurdle
options.explanation: Correct. Excess = 12% − 8% = 4% of $200 million = $8 million. 20% × $8 million = $1.6 million.

item.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts incentive fees in hedge funds with carried interest in private equity funds?

options.text: Hedge fund fees can apply to unrealized gains, while PE carry is on realized exit gains
options.explanation: Correct. Hedge funds charge incentive fees on realized and unrealized gains, while PE carry is paid on gains from exited deals.

options.text: PE carry is charged on unrealized gains, while hedge fund fees use realized gains
options.explanation: Reverses the two structures.

options.text: Both are charged only on realized gains, and neither can include a hurdle rate
options.explanation: Wrong on both counts. Hedge funds can charge on unrealized gains, and hurdle rates are common in private equity.

item.stem: A hedge fund manager is paid an incentive fee that is treated as a call option on fund performance. The fund is far below its high-water mark. What behaviour does this structure most likely encourage?

options.text: Cutting risk sharply because further losses would reduce the management fee
options.explanation: Describes the behaviour expected when the fund is well above its high-water mark, where the manager's payoff becomes more symmetrical.

options.text: Ignoring risk entirely because only the management fee affects pay
options.explanation: The incentive fee is still a valuable option and affects behaviour even when the fund is under water.

options.text: Raising risk because a large gain could earn a fee and losses cost little
options.explanation: Correct. Option-like payoffs gain from volatility. The manager has little to lose and may gamble for a fee.

item.stem: Which statement best compares typical management fee bases in closed-end and evergreen private credit funds?

options.text: Both charge only on NAV, since closed-end funds have no commitments
options.explanation: Closed-end funds are built on LP commitments, so the fee base is not simply NAV.

options.text: Closed-end: committed capital early, then invested cost; evergreen: invested capital or NAV
options.explanation: Correct. Closed-end funds usually charge on commitments during the investment period and later on invested cost. Evergreen funds charge on invested capital or NAV.

options.text: Closed-end: NAV throughout; evergreen: committed capital for the fund's life
options.explanation: Reverses the pattern. Evergreen funds have ongoing subscriptions and redemptions, so a NAV-based fee fits them better.

item.front: In a fund limited partnership, how do the GP and LPs differ?
item.back: The GP manages the fund and has unlimited liability. LPs supply capital, do not manage, and can lose only their investment.
A 2% annual management fee on assets plus a 20% incentive fee on profits. Large investors often negotiate lower terms.

item.front: Hard hurdle vs. soft hurdle: how does each affect the incentive fee?
item.back: Hard hurdle: the fee applies only to profit above the hurdle. Soft hurdle: once the hurdle is beaten, the fee applies to all profit (full catch-up).
A term that makes the GP return carry paid early to the LPs if later losses mean the GP received more than its share of whole-fund profits.

item.front: What does a high-water mark do?
item.back: It requires NAV to recover above its previous peak before a new incentive fee is earned, so investors do not pay twice for the same gains.
